summary: This informational RFC gives detailed call flows showing how the Centralized Conferencing Manipulation Protocol (RFC 6503) is used between a conference client and a conference server. The flows follow the scenarios in the XCON framework (RFC 5239) and in RFC 4597, and serve as worked examples for implementers.

eli5.summary: This is a book of sample conversations between a meeting app and a meeting server. Seeing who says what and in which order helps programmers get their own apps right.

questions: how does a conference client talk to the server
subtitle: Detailed examples of client-server message exchanges for conference control.

tldr.problem: The Centralized Conferencing Manipulation Protocol (CCMP) defines how to control conferences, but without practical examples, implementers lack guidance on how to use the protocol for common scenarios.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides detailed call flows showing request-response exchanges between a conference control client (CMCC) and a conference server (ConfS) for creating, modifying, and managing conferences. The flows cover conference creation, adding participants, managing sidebars, and removing participants, with message bodies showing actual XML.
tldr.outcome: Protocol developers and implementers can reference these worked examples to understand how CCMP messages are structured and sequenced for real-world conferencing operations.

today: RFC 6504 is an Informational specification providing call flow examples for CCMP (RFC 6503) and the XCON framework. It is not obsoleted and serves as the primary reference for understanding how to use CCMP in practice. The document remains essential for implementers of conferencing systems and SIP-based unified communications platforms.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC provides detailed call flows for scenarios described in the Centralized Conferencing Framework (XCON, RFC 5239) and XCON scenarios (RFC 4597). The flows demonstrate how a Conference and Media Control Client (CMCC) communicates with a Conference Server (ConfS) using the Centralized Conferencing Manipulation Protocol (CCMP, RFC 6503).

The flows show the perspective of protocol communication alone, omitting details of media control (RFC 5567), SIP call signaling (RFC 3261), and Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP, RFC 4582), though the flows note where these protocols are invoked. This informational document serves both protocol researchers and developers implementing conferencing systems.

Unlike earlier media control examples, these flows are specific to the XML-based CCMP protocol and show how clients retrieve blueprints, create conferences, add users, and manage sidebars and floor control.
sections.eli5: This RFC shows lots of examples of what a meeting app asks a meeting server, and what the server replies. It helps programmers learn the right words to say and in what order.

sections.title: CCMP and the Data Model
sections.content:
CCMP is a stateless request-response protocol built on XML. The data model (RFC 6501) defines the structure of conference objects, including their attributes, users, media, floor control policies, and sidebars. A CMCC sends a CCMP request via HTTPS POST with a Content-Type header of 'application/ccmp+xml'. The ConfS parses the request, manipulates the conference object according to the data model constraints, and replies with a 200 OK response containing the result.

Every CCMP request includes a <confUserID> (identifying the requester), a <confObjID> (identifying the target conference), and an <operation> element (retrieve, create, update, or delete). The response includes a response code (200 for success) and optionally a <confInfo> element containing the conference object data.

Some fields in the data model are mandatory but must be generated by the server (like a conference's entity ID). For these, clients use a placeholder wildcard like 'AUTO_GENERATE_1' that the ConfS replaces with an actual value. This ensures compliance with the data model while allowing clients to request creation of new objects.
sections.eli5: CCMP is like filling out a form and mailing it. You say who you are, which conference you want to change, and what you want to do. The server fills in the form, changes the conference, and mails back the updated information.

sections.title: Transport and Notifications
sections.content:
CCMP requires HTTP/TLS (HTTPS) as the transport mechanism. A CMCC sends requests as HTTPS POST messages to a server-provided endpoint, and the ConfS replies with 200 OK responses. Both request and response bodies are CCMP messages in 'application/ccmp+xml' format. This ensures secure, stateless, and simple client-server interaction.

The XCON framework defines a notification protocol to inform clients of conference state changes. When SIP is used for call signaling, the XCON event package (RFC 6502) extends the SIP event package for conference state (RFC 4575). A SIP client sends SUBSCRIBE to subscribe to conference notifications; the server responds with NOTIFY messages whenever the conference changes. The call flows in this RFC note when notifications occur but do not show SIP messaging details, assuming the reader understands SIP.

Conference operations trigger both CCMP and media control interactions. When a CMCC creates a conference, the ConfS also communicates with a media server (MS) via media control protocol (RFC 5567) to create the actual conference mix. The call flows annotate these as 'media control' operations (a), (b), (c), and so on.
sections.eli5: Everything goes over HTTPS to be secure. The server tells clients about changes using SIP NOTIFY messages if they are listening. Behind the scenes, the server also talks to a media server to actually make the conference real.

sections.title: Conference Creation and Management
sections.content:
A conference can be created in several ways. The simplest is a client sending a confRequest message with <operation>create and no other configuration; the server creates a default conference and returns its identity and full configuration. Clients can also create conferences from blueprints, predefined conference templates. A client requests a list of blueprints filtered by XPath (e.g., 'show me blueprints with audio and video'), selects one, requests its details, and finally sends a confRequest/create message referencing the blueprint's ID. The server clones the blueprint to create the conference.

Once a conference exists, clients can add participants in several ways: sending an invite-only access list, allowing users to self-join, or having the server dial out to specific addresses. Users can be muted, can request floor control (for speaking rights), and can join sidebars (private conversations within the conference). The call flows show XML messages for each operation, demonstrating how clients add users with <userID> and <endpoint> elements, mute them with boolean flags, and manage floor control with <floor-request-handling> policies.

Sidebars are private sub-conferences. Internal sidebars involve a subset of the main conference participants; external sidebars involve new endpoints. Call flows show the CCMP messages for sidebar creation, private messaging within sidebars, coaching (where a coach monitors and communicates with a participant), and observing (where an observer views a sidebar but does not participate).
sections.eli5: Making a conference: send 'create' and get a default one, or pick a template first. Adding people: give their IDs and email addresses. Managing them: mute, give them speaking rights, or add them to side conversations. All this is done by sending XML messages and getting XML back.

sections.title: Messaging Details and Flows
sections.content:
Each call flow in the RFC includes a ladder diagram showing the sequence of messages and a detailed XML dump of the actual CCMP and media control messages. For example, the basic conference creation flow shows a CMCC sending a confRequest with <confUserID>Alice@example.com, the server creating the conference object and media mix via media control interactions (labeled A1, A2, etc.), and responding with a confResponse containing the new conference's XCON-URI and full configuration.

The flows show that the <version> field in the response increments when a conference is updated, allowing clients to detect stale data. Some responses may omit the full <confInfo> for efficiency; clients can retrieve it later with a confRequest/retrieve. The examples illustrate optional parameters: the 'method' attribute on <target> can be 'dial-out' to have the server initiate calls to users, 'dialed-in' if users call in, or a mix.

The RFC covers edge cases such as password-protected conferences (with <password> elements), DTMF monitoring for conferencing commands, recording and announcements (via IVR interactions), and removing participants or deleting entire conferences. Each scenario shows how a client initiates the operation, what messages the server exchanges with the media server, and what response the client receives.
sections.eli5: The flows show exact message examples with real XML. You see the ladder diagram (who sends what, in what order) and then the actual message text. This makes it clear what each field means and how to build your own messages.
